source.svs_title: A 3D View of an Atmospheric River from an Earth System Model
source.visualizer: Greg Shirah (NASA/GSFC), Horace Mitchell (NASA/GSFC), Cindy Starr (GST), Kel Elkins (USRA); scientists Allison Collow (UMBC), Natalie Thomas (UMBC), Michael Bosilovich (NASA/GSFC)
source.dataset: MERRA-2 reanalysis, hourly (NASA GMAO); GTOPO30 topography (USGS)

frames.label: Clouds over the whole Earth
frames.place: the whole Earth, with the Pacific in front
frames.alt: The Earth seen from space, wrapped in swirling white clouds over the Pacific and the Americas.
frames.story: Ten weeks of clouds from NASA's weather reanalysis, from the first of October, sped up so that each soft pulse is a new day. The pulses race: time is flying. There is no blue vapour yet, so the hum is quiet.

frames.label: Moisture leaves the tropics
frames.place: the central Pacific, north of the equator
frames.alt: The clouds fade and the Pacific turns teal and blue with water vapour; a yellow arrow traces moist air leaving the tropics and curving north.
frames.story: The clouds fade and the water vapour appears: teal where there is a little, deep blue where there is a lot. Near the equator, the trade winds pile up warm, moist air. Some of it breaks away and heads north. Listen for the hum growing.

frames.label: An atmospheric river forms
frames.place: the North Pacific, from Hawaii towards the United States
frames.span: 8 to 14 December 2010, as NASA's clock jumps back 2 times
frames.alt: A long, narrow band of deep blue vapour stretches from near Hawaii towards California, beside a large H for high pressure.
frames.story: Moisture from the tropics joins other streams into one long, narrow band: an atmospheric river. This one starts near Hawaii, so it is called a Pineapple Express, and it points at California. Each kalimba note is the river's deep-blue core crossing the picture.

frames.label: Along the river, in 3D
frames.place: the river itself, flying low along it
frames.span: 11 December 2010 at 18:43 UTC, NASA's clock standing still
frames.alt: The camera drops low and flies along the river: a thick, glowing blue band of vapour with white wind streaks racing over it.
frames.story: NASA stops the clock at 18:43 on 11 December 2010 and flies the camera low along the river. The pulses stop. Look at the river from the side: most of its vapour stays close to the ocean surface.

frames.label: Steered by high and low pressure
frames.ariaLabel: Steered by high and low pressure
frames.place: the North Pacific, between a high off California and a low near Alaska
frames.span: 10 to 14 December 2010, as NASA's clock jumps back 4 times
frames.alt: From a low angle over the ocean, the blue river runs between a high-pressure H and a low-pressure L, towards the coast.
frames.story: Two weather systems steer the river: a high off California and Mexico, and a low near Alaska. Between them the winds squeeze the moisture into a narrow corridor. The stronger the difference in pressure, the stronger the winds, and the heavier the rain that follows. The clock replays the same days several times as the camera moves.

frames.label: Orographic lift over the mountains
frames.place: the coast and mountains of California, near Lake Tahoe
frames.span: 11 to 14 December 2010, as NASA's clock jumps back 2 times
frames.alt: The river meets California's coast; the moist air rises over steep, snowy mountains, with the label orographic lift.
frames.story: The river reaches the coast and runs into the mountains. The air is forced up, cools, and its water falls as rain, and as snow higher up, mostly on the slopes facing the ocean. This is orographic lift. It fills reservoirs and snowpack, but a strong river can bring floods and mudslides.

frames.label: The river reaches the West Coast
frames.ariaLabel: The river reaches the West Coast
frames.place: the west coast of North America
frames.span: 11 to 14 December 2010, as NASA's clock jumps back 5 times
frames.alt: Looking down on the west coast of North America: a blue river of vapour reaches the coast between the H and the L.
frames.story: From higher up, you can see the whole river land on the West Coast, again and again as the clock replays 11 to 14 December. Every pass carries more moisture to the mountains.

frames.label: Atmospheric rivers around the world
frames.place: the whole Earth as it turns
frames.span: 3 to 14 December 2010, as NASA's clock jumps back 2 times
frames.alt: The camera pulls back to the whole Earth; it turns past Asia, Africa and the Americas, with blue streaks of vapour over every ocean.
frames.story: The camera pulls back and the Earth turns. Atmospheric rivers are not only a Pacific story: they also reach Europe, New Zealand, the Middle East, Greenland and Antarctica. NASA's weather record has hourly data like this for the whole Earth, back to 1980.

legend.summary: NASA's 3D film of an atmospheric river in December 2010, from MERRA-2, a weather model that blends in satellite and weather station observations. A river of water vapour forms over the tropical Pacific and flows to the mountains of California.
legend.method: The picture is read in bands, top to bottom: the top sounds higher and in your left ear, the bottom lower and in your right. The hum is all the water vapour in the picture: soft over dry air, full where the vapour piles up. Where the river's deep-blue core crosses a band, a kalimba note falls like a drop. A soft low pulse marks each midnight on NASA's clock, so you hear time race, stop and repeat.

items.meaning: The river's core, the deepest blue and the most water vapour, crossing that height of the picture. Louder = more of it.
All the water vapour in the picture. It is soft over dry air and grows where vapour piles up.
One soft pulse each time NASA's clock passes midnight. Fast pulses: weeks flying by. No pulses: NASA has stopped the clock.

legend.caveat: Values are read from the blue shading in NASA's picture, so they are relative, not tonnes of water. Only water vapour is read. In this 3D film the rain is drawn under the see-through vapour, which makes its colours look like sunlit land, so rain, snow and soil moisture are not read. The camera moves, so the scenes say where it is. The dates are NASA's own, read from its date overlay: the clock races through October and November, replays 10 to 14 December several times, and stops at 11 December, 18:43 UTC, while the camera flies along the river.
